uncited: It solves the problem of redundant intersection tests in dense scenes by skipping empty space, reducing the number of primitive intersection checks [3950-regular-grid].

Unlike [Voxel Grid Raycasting](2218-voxel-grid-raycasting.md) which typically renders volumetric density, this method accelerates geometric ray tracing by storing primitive pointers in voxels [3950-regular-grid].

It differs from [Hierarchical Grid Traversal](52-name.md) by using a flat, uniform structure without hierarchical levels, and from [Sparse Voxel Traversal](5228-sparse-voxel-tracing.md) by not using sparse data structures like octrees [3950-regular-grid].

The family shares the mechanism of 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3D-DDA) traversal to step through a uniform 3D grid [4091-voxel-based-ray-tracing-for-gi-and-specular-reflections, 4240-optimised-voxel-ray-marching].
The grid partitions the scene's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) into $N^3$ uniform cells [3950-regular-grid].

Rays are advanced by calculating the distance to the next cell boundary along each axis, advancing the coordinate with the smallest distance [3950-regular-grid, 4091-voxel-based-ray-tracing-for-gi-and-specular-reflections].
The traversal stops when the ray exits the grid bounds or finds a primitive intersection [3950-regular-grid].

Finally, it notes that 'grid traversal must find all cells traversed by the ray segment' (implied by the context of returning all voxels and the unsuitability of Bresenham because it misses pixels). Regular Grid Traversal is a ray-grid traversal method that accelerates ray-primitive intersection tests by mapping primitives to a uniform 3D voxel grid and stepping through occupied cells using 3D-DDA [S1, 3950-regular-grid].

The claim states that Regular Grid Traversal is a ray-grid traversal method that accelerates intersection tests by mapping primitives to a uniform 3D voxel grid and stepping through occupied cells using 3D-DDA. The evidence in Source [S1] confirms that grid traversal algorithms return all voxels (cells) traversed by a ray, where each cell is associated with a subset of primitives (mapping primitives to the grid). It also describes the process of advancing from a cell to its neighbor (stepping through cells) and explicitly discusses the use of traversal algorithms for this purpose. While the specific term '3D-DDA' is not explicitly named in the provided snippets, the description of the algorithm (finding all cells traversed by a parametric ray, stepping through neighbors, distinguishing from Bresenham) is the standard definition of the 3D-DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer) algorithm used in grid traversal. The evidence supports the core functional description of the method.
